title: Research Ethics
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Research Ethics. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Research ethics protects people’s dignity, agency, privacy, and safety. Participants need understandable information about purpose, activities, recording, data use, risks, compensation, and their right to stop. Consent is an ongoing choice, not a checkbox collected once.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Collect only what is necessary, protect it appropriately, and avoid exposing people to avoidable discomfort or consequences. Plan for power imbalances and sensitive contexts. An employee, patient, student, or financially vulnerable participant may not feel equally free to refuse. Ethical research improves evidence because people can participate knowingly and safely.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at ethics continues after the session?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: In synthesis, the team avoids turning one painful story into emotional theatre. Clips require permission and limited audience. Findings describe structural conditions without stereotyping people as vulnerable or noncompliant. When research identifies a harmful status message, the team assigns an owner and interim protection rather than waiting for the final report.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Design protection through the whole research lifecycle
turns.text: What changes when we look at design protection through the whole research lifecycle?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Risk is situational. Discussing delayed care may cause distress; a helper may reveal another person’s information; screen recordings may capture medical data; staff may fear performance consequences. The plan includes stop rules, signposting, secure handling, role-limited access, anonymisation limits, and a route for unexpected safety concerns.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Participants learn how findings were used; lived experience is not extracted as decorative evidence.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at design participant protection?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Assess purpose, necessity, vulnerability, power, sensitivity, burden, potential harm, and benefit. Make participation voluntary with understandable consent, ability to pause or withdraw, proportionate incentive, accessible materials, and honest explanation of recording and data use.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Minimise collection and access. Define storage, retention, deletion, de-identification limits, vendors, and incident response before sessions. Protect confidentiality in notes, clips, repositories, and stakeholder presentations. Distinctive stories can re-identify even without names.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Plan for distress, disclosure, unsafe situations, and research that uncovers product harm. Researchers need escalation and duty-of-care guidance. Ethics continues through analysis and storytelling: avoid stereotyping, extractive participation, fabricated certainty, and recommendations that increase burden on people with least power.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Ethical risk should influence method choice and study scope. A fast study is not a success if it creates harm, captures data the organisation cannot steward, or produces consent people did not understand.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Ethics is embedded in the study design. Choose tasks, questions, recording, and storage practices that are proportionate to the benefit of learning. Explain what will happen in language people can understand, avoid collecting sensitive material “just in case,” and separate participation from any service, employment, education, or payment decision that could create pressure.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: When research involves trauma, health, financial hardship, identity, or legal status, build in specialist review, support, and safer alternatives.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Consent must remain meaningful throughout the session. A person should be able to skip a question, stop recording, withdraw, or take a break without being penalised. Protect confidentiality in recruitment, observation, analysis, reporting, and playback. Share findings in a way that preserves context without making an individual identifiable to people who do not need to know.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Checkbox consent: a dense form replaces a genuine explanation and choice. Coercive context: participants believe service or employment depends on cooperation. Data excess: recordings and identifiers are retained without a defined need or owner. Extractive research: people share difficult experiences but receive no respect, support, or influence.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A diary study of financial hardship can create privacy and emotional risk even when no medical data is involved. Minimising prompts, enabling skips, separating incentives from completion, and planning deletion are research-design decisions.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Sampling decides who is included. Ethics determines how the team earns the right to learn from them. lesson 24 then teaches how to state the resulting evidence with appropriate confidence.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Review a sign-up flow. What would a participant need to know before agreeing to a study or data collection activity?
